title: Infrastructure as Code with Terraform
intro: Up to now you made containers by typing commands. From here on you describe infrastructure in files, and Terraform makes the real world match them. Four days run on Docker on your laptop and take the language, state and modules slowly, with real plans to read. The fifth day takes the same skills to AWS and GitHub Actions, and that part is optional.

lessons.title: Infrastructure as Code and your first Terraform
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain why teams write infrastructure as code, read a Terraform plan, and create, change and destroy a container with Terraform on your laptop.

guess.q: You run `terraform apply`, it succeeds, and then you run `terraform apply` again without changing any file. What happens the second time?
options: It creates a second copy of everything
It reports no changes and does nothing
It deletes everything and creates it again
It fails because the things already exist
guess.why: Terraform compares your files with what already exists. When they match there is nothing to do, so running it again is safe.

sections.h: Why clicking in a console does not scale
sections.body:
Every cloud has a web console. You can click a server, a database and a network into existence in ten minutes, and it works. Six months later you need the same setup again for a test environment. Which boxes did you tick? Nobody remembers, and nobody wrote it down.

Doing infrastructure by hand goes wrong in three ways:
- You cannot repeat it. There is no exact copy for testing, for another region, or for recovery after a disaster.
- Nobody reviews it. A change happens without a second pair of eyes, and nothing records who did what.
- It drifts. Someone changes a setting by hand during an incident, and reality slowly moves away from what the team believes.

**Infrastructure as Code** (IaC) means you describe your infrastructure in text files, and a tool makes the real world match them. The files live in git next to your app, so infrastructure gets the same treatment as your Kotlin code:
- `git log` shows every change, who made it and why.
- A pull request lets a teammate review a change before it reaches anything real.
- Reverting a commit and applying again rolls a change back.
- The same files build a second, identical environment.

The short version: your infrastructure gets a pull request. This part of the course uses Terraform, the most widely used IaC tool. You practise on Docker on your laptop for four days, so nothing costs money. Day 29 is the optional trip to a real cloud.

sections.h: Declarative: describe the result, not the steps
sections.body:
You can tell a computer what you want in two ways:
- Imperative: you list the steps. "Pull nginx, then start a container, then publish port 8090." A shell script works this way.
- Declarative: you describe the result. "There is one nginx container called tf-web on port 8090." The tool works out the steps.

Terraform is declarative, and you feel the difference the second time you run it. Run a `docker run` script twice and the second run fails, because the name is taken. Run Terraform twice and the second run prints `No changes`. The file only says what should exist, and it already does. A command that gives the same result however many times you run it is called idempotent.

As a backend engineer you already know this idea from SQL. You write `SELECT ... WHERE status = 'PAID'`, and the database decides whether to use an index or scan the table. Terraform is similar. You write the end state, and Terraform makes a plan of API calls to get there. Under the hood it still runs steps in order. You just do not write them.

You met the same idea on Day 15. `compose.yaml` describes services, and `docker compose up` makes them exist. Compose only knows Docker on one machine. Terraform talks to almost anything that has an API: Docker, AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, GitHub, Cloudflare and thousands more.

sections.h: Terraform, OpenTofu and the other tools
sections.body:
HashiCorp makes Terraform, and IBM bought HashiCorp in February 2025. Terraform was open source under the MPL licence until August 2023. Then [HashiCorp moved it to the Business Source License](https://www.hashicorp.com/en/blog/hashicorp-adopts-business-source-license) (BSL). You may still use Terraform for free at work. What you may not do is sell a product that competes with HashiCorp's own.

Part of the community disliked the change and forked the last open source version. The fork is called OpenTofu. It lives at the Linux Foundation and joined the CNCF in 2025. You type `tofu` instead of `terraform`, and `tofu plan` behaves like `terraform plan`. The language is the same, and everything in this part works with both. A few newer features exist in only one of them. If your team already uses one, stay with it.

You will hear about these tools too:
- CloudFormation: AWS's own IaC service, with YAML or JSON templates. It works only for AWS.
- Pulumi: IaC written in normal languages such as TypeScript, Python, Go, C# or Java.
- Ansible: connects to servers that already exist and sets them up (packages, files, services).

Teams often combine them. Terraform creates the network, the machines and the Kubernetes cluster. A container image or Ansible decides what runs inside. Terraform can configure servers too, but that is not where it shines.

sections.h: Providers, resources and the shape of a .tf file
sections.body:
Terraform files end in `.tf` and use HCL, the HashiCorp Configuration Language. Terraform reads every `.tf` file in a folder as one configuration, so file names are only for humans. A file is made of blocks:
- A block has a type, labels and braces: `resource "docker_container" "web" { }`.
- An argument sets a value inside a block: `name = "tf-web"`.
- A reference reads a value from another block: `docker_image.nginx.image_id`.

A **provider** is a plugin that translates your blocks into API calls for one platform. The `terraform` block lists the providers you need, with a source and a version, much like a dependency in `build.gradle.kts`. This lesson uses `kreuzwerker/docker`, which talks to the same Docker engine as the `docker` command. The `provider "docker" {}` block then configures it. Empty braces mean "use the defaults".

A resource block has two labels. The first is the resource type, such as `docker_container`, and it always starts with the provider's name. The second is your own name for it, such as `web`. Together they make the address `docker_container.web`. The address must be unique in the folder, and Terraform uses it everywhere: in plans, in state and in commands.

References also set the order. The container refers to the image, so Terraform pulls the image first. You never write "do this first". Resources with no reference between them are created in parallel.

sections.h: The workflow: init, plan, apply, destroy
sections.body:
You use the same few commands every day, in this order:
1. `terraform init` downloads the providers into a hidden `.terraform` folder and writes `.terraform.lock.hcl`. Run it once per folder, and again after you add a provider or module.
2. `terraform fmt` tidies the layout of your files, and `terraform validate` checks for typos and broken references. Neither touches anything real.
3. `terraform plan` compares your files, the state and the real world. It prints what it would do and changes nothing.
4. `terraform apply` makes a fresh plan, shows it, waits for you to type `yes`, makes the changes and updates the state.
5. `terraform destroy` removes everything this folder manages, after the same `yes`.

Plan is safe to run any time, so run it often. People sometimes worry that plan changes things. It does not. Apply is the only step that does.

There is one gap to know about. Apply makes a new plan, and the world may have changed since your last plan. For a laptop that does not matter. In a pipeline it does, so you save the plan with `terraform plan -out=tfplan` and later run `terraform apply tfplan`. Terraform then does exactly what you reviewed, or stops if the state moved on. Day 29 uses this.

`terraform destroy` deletes everything in this folder's state, not only what you added today. It never touches things the folder does not manage, such as a container you started by hand.

sections.h: Reading a plan
sections.body:
A plan lists every resource it would touch, each with a symbol in front:
- `+` create a new resource.
- `~` update in place: the same object stays, and a setting changes.
- `-/+` replace: destroy the old object, then create a new one.
- `-` destroy.

Three more things show up all the time. `(known after apply)` means the provider will only know the value once the object exists, like a container's ID. That is normal, not an error. `# (50 unchanged attributes hidden)` means Terraform left out the lines that do not change. The last line is the summary, such as `Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.`

Replacement is where people get hurt. Some settings cannot change on a running object. Docker cannot move a running container to a new host port, or give it new environment variables. A one-character edit to one of those becomes `-/+`, and the line that caused it ends with `# forces replacement`.

For an nginx container, replacement means a second of downtime. For a database it can mean an empty database. So build one habit now. Before you type `yes`, read the summary line and search the plan for `forces replacement`. If the numbers surprise you, stop and find out why.

sections.h: What init and apply leave behind
sections.body:
After your first apply, the folder holds three new things. Each has a different rule for git:
- `.terraform/` holds the downloaded provider binaries. It is a cache that `init` can always rebuild. Never commit it.
- `.terraform.lock.hcl` records the exact provider version and its checksums. Commit it, so your laptop, your teammates and CI all run the same provider code.
- `terraform.tfstate` is the state: Terraform's record of what it created. Never commit it.

State is how Terraform links the address `docker_container.web` to one real container ID. Without it, Terraform could not tell "create a container" from "this container already exists". State can also hold passwords in plain text, which is the main reason it stays out of git. Day 27 is all about state.

Two names sound alike, so keep them apart. The lock file pins provider versions. A state lock, which you meet on Day 27, stops two people from changing the same state at once.

The lab's `.gitignore` already blocks `.terraform/` and `*.tfstate`. GitHub keeps a [ready-made Terraform .gitignore](https://github.com/github/gitignore/blob/main/Terraform.gitignore) if you start a new repo.

lessons.analogy: Terraform works like a thermostat. You set the temperature you want, and it turns the heating on or off until the room matches. You never tell it "heat for ten minutes", and setting the same temperature twice does nothing. The comparison breaks in one place: a thermostat checks the room all the time, while Terraform only looks when you run plan or apply.

steps.say: Make a practice folder outside your repo and save the `main.tf` from the Files section in it. Then run init. It reads the `terraform` block and downloads the Docker provider. The output is trimmed.

$ mkdir -p ~/code/tf-first && cd ~/code/tf-first
$ terraform init

Initializing provider plugins...
- Finding kreuzwerker/docker versions matching "~> 4.6"...
- Installing kreuzwerker/docker v4.6.0...

steps.say: Preview. Nothing exists yet, so both resources get a `+`. The real plan lists about 40 attributes for the container; these are the ones worth reading. The ID and image are `(known after apply)` because Docker only knows them later.
steps.code:
$ terraform plan
  # docker_container.web will be created
  + resource "docker_container" "web" {
      + id                                          = (known after apply)
      + image                                       = (known after apply)
      + name                                        = "tf-web"
      + restart                                     = "no"
      + ports {
          + external = 8090
          + internal = 80
        }
    }
  # docker_image.nginx will be created
Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

steps.say: Apply. Terraform shows the plan again and waits for `yes`. The image comes first because the container refers to it. Then check that nginx answers.

docker_image.nginx: Creating...

lessons.mistake: Typing `yes` without reading the plan. A one-word edit can turn into `-/+`, and replacing a database means losing its data. Read the summary line and search for `forces replacement` every time, even when you are sure the change is small.
lessons.real_world: Take PayLoop, a payments company made up for this course. Nobody there creates production infrastructure by clicking. Every change is a pull request with the Terraform plan attached, and a second engineer reads the plan before anyone applies it. People open the cloud console to look around, or during an incident, and the next plan shows whatever they changed by hand.

task.title: Run Redis for hello-devops with Terraform
steps: In your hello-devops repo, create the folder `infra/local` and add `versions.tf` from the Files section.
Add a `main.tf` with two resources: a `docker_image` for `redis:8-alpine` with `keep_locally = true`, and a `docker_container` named `hello-redis` that uses it.
Run `terraform fmt`, `terraform init` and `terraform plan`. Before you read the summary line, predict it.
Apply, then check that Redis answers with `docker exec hello-redis redis-cli ping`.
Add `restart = "unless-stopped"` to the container and plan. Is it `~` or `-/+`? Apply it.
Change the container's name and plan again. Find the line that forces replacement, then change the name back without applying.
Run `ls -a` and `cat .terraform.lock.hcl`, then `git status`. Which new files does git offer to commit, and which does it ignore?
Run `terraform destroy`. Check with `docker ps -a` that the container is gone and with `docker image ls redis` that the image stayed.
Commit `versions.tf`, `main.tf` and `.terraform.lock.hcl`.
hints: The container's `image` argument should be a reference to the image resource's `image_id`, like in the nginx example.
Redis needs no published port today. `docker exec` runs `redis-cli` inside the container.
If Terraform cannot connect to Docker but `docker ps` works, run `docker context inspect` to find your socket, then set `DOCKER_HOST` to it.
task.done_when: `docker exec hello-redis redis-cli ping` printed PONG, `git status` shows no state file, and after `terraform destroy` the container is gone from `docker ps -a`.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate has never used Terraform. In 3 to 4 sentences, tell them what happens when you run `terraform plan` and then `terraform apply`. Mention the state file and what `-/+` means.
explain_back.answer: Plan reads my .tf files, the state file and the real world, then prints the difference without changing anything. Apply makes that plan again, asks me to confirm, and calls the provider to make the changes. Then it updates the state file, so next time Terraform knows what already exists. A `-/+` means a setting cannot change on the existing object, so Terraform destroys it and creates a new one.

recap: IaC means describing infrastructure in files, so you get review, history and repeatable setups.
Terraform is declarative and idempotent: you describe the result, and a second run changes nothing.
A resource address such as `docker_container.web` is the type plus your own name.
init downloads providers, plan previews, apply makes the changes, destroy cleans up.
Plan symbols: `+` create, `~` update in place, `-/+` replace, `-` destroy. Look for `forces replacement`.
Commit `.terraform.lock.hcl`; never commit `.terraform/` or `terraform.tfstate`.

check.q: You change only the `image` of a `docker_container` and run plan. The container shows `-/+`. What will apply do?
options: Edit the running container in place
Stop because the file has an error
Destroy the container and create a new one
Pull the new image but keep the old container
check.why: `-/+` means replace: a running container cannot switch images, so Terraform removes it and creates a new one.

check.q: A teammate deletes the `tf-web` container by hand. You run `terraform plan` without changing any file. What will the plan most likely show?
options: A create, to bring the container back
Nothing, because your files did not change
An error saying the state is broken
A destroy, to remove it from your files
check.why: Plan reads the real world, sees the container is missing, and proposes to create it again so reality matches the code.

check.q: You started a `db` container with `docker run` yesterday. Today you run `terraform destroy` in `~/code/tf-first`. What happens to `db`?
options: It is destroyed, because destroy removes all containers
Terraform asks whether to destroy it too
It is imported into the state first
Nothing, because this folder's state does not track it
check.why: Destroy only removes what this folder's state tracks; Terraform never learned about `db`.

interview.q: What is Infrastructure as Code, and why would a team use it?
interview.a: Infrastructure as Code means describing infrastructure, such as networks, servers and permissions, in text files that a tool applies. The files live in git, so every change gets reviewed and leaves a history. You can rebuild the same setup in another region or account, which helps testing and disaster recovery. It also exposes drift: the code is the source of truth, and a plan shows any difference.

interview.q: What is the difference between Terraform and Ansible?
interview.a: Terraform is declarative. It mainly creates infrastructure through cloud and platform APIs, and it tracks what it created in a state file. Ansible is mainly for configuration: it connects to existing machines over SSH and runs tasks such as installing packages, in order. Many teams use both. Terraform creates the machines, and Ansible or a container image decides what runs on them.

interview.q: What does `forces replacement` mean in a plan, and why does it matter?
interview.a: It marks an attribute that the provider cannot change on an existing object, so Terraform must destroy the object and create a new one. The plan shows the resource as `-/+`. For a stateless container that is a short blip. For a database or a disk it can mean data loss or downtime, so you read those lines before approving and look for a safer change if needed.

deeper.body:
Version constraints and the lock file decide which provider code runs on your machine. They deserve ten minutes, because a surprise upgrade can break a plan that worked yesterday.

The `version` argument in `required_providers` is a constraint, and three forms cover most needs:
- `= 4.6.0` allows exactly one version.
- `~> 4.6` allows 4.6 and newer, but stays below 5.0. This is the usual choice.
- `~> 4.6.0` allows 4.6.x patch releases only.

`~>` is called the pessimistic constraint: only the rightmost number you wrote may grow. Major versions can remove or rename things, so you move to a new major version on purpose, after reading the provider's upgrade guide. The [version constraints page](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/expressions/version-constraints) has the full syntax.

`terraform init` picks the newest version that fits and records it in `.terraform.lock.hcl`, together with checksums of the provider files. From then on, init installs that exact version, even when a newer one exists. To move forward, run `terraform init -upgrade`, read the plan, and commit the new lock file. Gradle users can think of it as a dependency lock that is on by default.

Mac users run into one edge case. Checksums are per platform: your Mac is `darwin_arm64`, while GitHub's runners are `linux_amd64`. A normal install from the public registry records checksums for every platform. When providers come from a local mirror or cache instead, init may record only your own platform, and init in CI then fails on the checksum. Terraform prints a warning when this happens. Fix it once with `terraform providers lock -platform=darwin_arm64 -platform=linux_amd64`, which records both, and commit the result.

The `terraform` block can also hold `required_version`, which sets the Terraform CLI versions allowed to run the code. The lab's `infra/local` asks for `>= 1.10`, and `infra/aws` asks for `>= 1.11` because the S3 lock file you meet on Day 29 needs it.

OpenTofu reads the same blocks but downloads providers from its own registry. Read the OpenTofu migration guide before you switch one state between `terraform` and `tofu`, and keep a backup of the state while you try it.

lessons.goal: By the end you can write Terraform with typed variables, locals, outputs and expressions, try any expression in terraform console, and choose between count and for_each.

guess.q: You made three containers with `count` from the list ["alpha", "bravo", "charlie"]. You delete "alpha" from the list. What does the next plan do?
options: Destroys only the alpha container
Nothing until you apply twice
Replaces two copies and destroys a third
Renames the alpha container to bravo
guess.why: With `count`, each copy is known by its position. Every name after alpha moves up one place, so copies [0] and [1] get new content and are replaced, and [2] is destroyed.

terms.plain: Any piece of HCL that produces a value, such as "web-${var.name}" or var.port + 1.
A named, typed setting a Terraform folder accepts, read as var.NAME.
A named expression inside one folder, read as local.NAME, used to avoid repeating yourself.
A value a folder hands back after apply, shown by terraform output.
An expression that builds a new list or map from an existing one, like map and filter in Kotlin.
A meta-argument that makes a number of copies of a resource, known as [0], [1] and so on.
A meta-argument that makes one copy of a resource per key in a map or set, known as ["key"].

sections.h: HCL is configuration with expressions
sections.body:
On Day 25 every value was a literal: a fixed string or number. Real configurations compute values. An expression is any piece of HCL that produces a value: a literal like `8080`, a reference like `var.host_port`, a template like `"http://localhost:${var.host_port}"`, or a function call like `upper("hi")`.

References are how one block reads another. You will use these forms all the time:
- `var.NAME` reads an input variable.
- `local.NAME` reads a local value.
- `TYPE.NAME.ATTRIBUTE` reads a resource, as in `docker_container.redis.name`.
- `each.key`, `each.value` and `count.index` exist inside resources that use `for_each` or `count`.
- `path.module` is the folder the current `.tf` file lives in.

HCL looks like a programming language, but it behaves more like a spreadsheet. Nothing runs top to bottom, you never reassign a variable, and there are no loops with side effects. Terraform reads every block, follows the references to build a graph, and works out each value once its inputs are known. That is why the order of blocks in a file does not matter.

The fastest way to learn expressions is to try them. `terraform console` opens a prompt, like `jshell` or the Kotlin REPL, where you type an expression and see its value. Inside a folder it also knows that folder's variables, locals and state. You can pipe in one expression too: `echo 'upper("hi")' | terraform console`. Every example in this lesson was checked that way.

sections.h: Types: from strings to objects
sections.body:
Every value has a type, and Terraform checks types before it touches anything. There are three families:
- Primitive types hold one value: `string`, `number` and `bool`.
- Collection types hold many values of one type. `list(string)` is ordered, `set(string)` has no order and no duplicates, and `map(number)` has string keys.
- Structural types mix types. `object({ name = string, port = number })` has named fields, and `tuple([string, number])` is a fixed row of positions.

`null` means "no value". Setting an argument to `null` is the same as leaving it out.

Two things surprise newcomers. First, a literal in square brackets is a tuple, not a list, and a literal in braces is an object, not a map. Ask the console for `type(["b", "a"])` and it says `tuple([string, string])`. Terraform converts it to a list or a map when a variable's type asks for one, so you rarely notice.

Second, Terraform converts between primitives for you. `"8080" + 1` gives `8081`. Put the number 8080 into a `map(string)` and it becomes the string `"8080"`. When a conversion is impossible, such as `"abc"` where a number belongs, you get an error at plan time, before anything changes.

Sets matter later in this lesson. `toset(["b", "a", "b"])` gives `["a", "b"]`: the duplicate is gone, and Terraform chose the order.

sections.h: Input variables: defaults, validation and sensitive
sections.body:
A `variable` block declares a setting the folder accepts. Look at `host_port` in the lab's new `variables.tf` in the Files section. It has four parts:
- `description` explains the variable to the next person.
- `type` rejects wrong values early: `number` here.
- `default` makes the variable optional. Without one, Terraform asks you for a value.
- `validation` adds your own rule, with a `condition` and an `error_message`.

Pass `-var host_port=80` and the plan stops before anything runs, with `host_port must be between 1024 and 65535.` Validation is the cheapest place to catch a bad input.

`sensitive = true` hides a value in plan and apply output, which then shows `(sensitive value)`. It encrypts nothing. The value still lands in the state file in plain text, as Day 27 shows.

A value can come from several places. When two of them set the same variable, the later one in this list wins. Each step was checked in the console:
1. The `default` in the variable block.
2. An environment variable, such as `TF_VAR_host_port=9001`.
3. A `terraform.tfvars` file, then `terraform.tfvars.json`, loaded automatically.
4. Any `*.auto.tfvars` files, in alphabetical order.
5. The `-var` and `-var-file` flags, in the order you type them.

The `-var` flag has a trap: Terraform does not remember it. Apply with `-var host_port=8081` today, plan without it tomorrow, and the plan moves the app back to 8080. Put values you always want in a `.tfvars` file.

sections.h: Locals and outputs
sections.body:
Locals are named expressions inside one folder. You write them in a `locals` block and read them as `local.NAME`. Think of a `val` inside a Kotlin function: computed once, named, and read many times. The lab's `main.tf` now uses one called `app_env` to build the app's settings in one place.

Use locals to remove repetition or to give a hard expression a name. HashiCorp's style guide says to use them sparingly, because a reader has to jump around to find each one. If a value should change between runs, make it a variable instead.

Outputs are the folder's return values. Apply prints them at the end, and later you read them again:
- `terraform output` prints all of them.
- `terraform output -raw url` prints one string without quotes, handy in `curl $(terraform output -raw url)`.
- `terraform output -json` prints them for tools like `jq`.

Outputs matter even more on Day 28. A module, a folder that another folder calls, can hand values back only through outputs. An output can be `sensitive` too, and then the CLI prints `<sensitive>` instead of the value.

sections.h: Strings, conditionals and for expressions
sections.body:
Most expressions you write are one of four kinds. String templates put values into text: `"http://localhost:${var.host_port}"`. Inside a string, `%{ if }` and `%{ for }` directives add logic, so `"%{ for n in ["a", "b"] }
  • ${n}
    • %{ endfor }"` gives `
  • a
  • b
    • `. For text over several lines, a heredoc starts with `<<-EOT` and ends with `EOT`. A conditional picks one of two values: `var.greeting == "" ? "app default" : var.greeting`. Both results must have the same type. The lab uses one to add `GREETING` only when you set it. A for expression builds a new collection from an old one. If you know Kotlin's `map`, `filter` and `associateWith`, you already know it: - `[for n in var.names : upper(n)]` is like `names.map { it.uppercase() }`. - `[for n in var.names : n if n != "bravo"]` is like `names.filter { it != "bravo" }`. - `{for n in var.names : n => length(n)}` is like `names.associateWith { it.length }`. Square brackets build a list and braces build a map. A splat is a shortcut for one common case: `local_file.by_count[*].filename` is the list of every copy's `filename`. Built-in functions finish the toolbox: `merge`, `lookup`, `join`, `format`, `cidrsubnet`, `try` and many more. You cannot write your own functions. That keeps configurations predictable, and it is also why some expressions grow long.

sections.h: Copies with count and for_each, and the trap between them
sections.body:
Expressions transform values. To make several copies of a resource you need a meta-argument, an argument that Terraform itself reads on any resource.

`count` takes a number. `count = 3` makes three copies with the addresses `local_file.by_count[0]`, `[1]` and `[2]`, and `count.index` tells each copy its number.

`for_each` takes a map or a set of strings, and each key becomes one copy, with an address like `docker_container.site["blue"]`. Inside the block, `each.key` is the key and `each.value` is the value. A plain list is rejected with `Invalid for_each argument`, so wrap it in `toset()`.

This trips most people up: the address is the copy's identity. With `count`, the identity is a position. Remove the first name from a list of three, and every later name moves up one place. Copy `[0]` now holds what `[1]` held, so its content changes and it is replaced. The same happens to `[1]`, and `[2]` is destroyed. With `for_each`, the identity is the name, so only the removed copy goes. The worked example shows the real plan.

The docs give a rule of thumb. Use `count` for nearly identical copies, or as an on-off switch such as `count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0`. Use `for_each` when each copy has its own name or settings. The style guide adds: use both sparingly.

One more limit applies to both. Terraform must know the count or the keys at plan time, so they cannot come from an attribute that only exists after apply.

sections.h: Dynamic blocks: a loop inside one resource
sections.body:
`for_each` copies a whole resource. Sometimes you want copies of a block inside one resource instead, such as several `ports` blocks on one container. A `dynamic` block does that:

`dynamic "ports" { for_each = var.port_map  content { internal = tonumber(ports.key)  external = ports.value } }`

With `port_map = { "80" = 8091, "8080" = 8092 }`, the plan shows two `ports` blocks, and Docker publishes both ports on one container. Inside `content`, the loop variable is named after the block, so you write `ports.key` and `ports.value`.

Use dynamic blocks rarely. The docs warn that overuse makes configuration hard to read, and they suggest writing nested blocks out by hand wherever you can. Two `ports` blocks typed out are easier to review than a loop that builds them.

lessons.analogy: A Terraform configuration is like a spreadsheet. Variables are input cells, locals and outputs are formula cells, and a formula can refer to any other cell. Change one input and everything that depends on it is worked out again, and you never say in which order. The comparison breaks because some of Terraform's "cells" are real containers: a changed formula can replace one.

8080, because the default always wins
None: Terraform asks you to choose
check.why: A `terraform.tfvars` file beats a `TF_VAR_` environment variable, and both beat the default.

Terraform skips that entry
The value becomes null
Terraform converts it to the number 8081

Use `count = var.names` instead
Add `depends_on = [var.names]`
Mark the variable as sensitive

interview.q: When do you use count and when for_each?
interview.a: Both create several copies of a resource. The `count` argument numbers the copies, so it fits identical copies or an on-off switch like `count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0`. The `for_each` argument keys each copy by a map key or set value, so it fits copies with their own names or settings. I default to `for_each` for anything named, because removing an item from a `count` list shifts the later copies and Terraform replaces them.

interview.q: How do you give one Terraform configuration different values per environment?
interview.a: I declare typed input variables with validation, and keep the per-environment values in files such as `dev.tfvars` and `prod.tfvars`, passed with `-var-file`. Secrets do not go in those files; they come from a secret store or CI at run time. Each environment also needs its own state, so I usually give each one its own root folder that calls shared modules. I avoid `-var` for anything permanent, because Terraform does not remember it.

interview.q: What is the difference between a variable, a local and an output?
interview.a: A variable is an input that the caller or the command line can set. A local is a named expression inside the folder that nobody outside can set, used to avoid repeating a long expression. An output is a value the folder hands back, printed after apply and readable by a parent module or a script. In function terms: parameters, local vals and return values.

deeper.body:
Say you already have resources built with `count`, and you want to move to `for_each` before the index trap bites. Simply editing the block is not enough. Terraform sees `[0]`, `[1]` and `[2]` vanish and `["alpha"]`, `["bravo"]` and `["charlie"]` appear, so it plans to destroy three and create three. The real plan says `local_file.greeting[0] will be destroyed (because resource does not use count)` and ends with `Plan: 3 to add, 0 to change, 3 to destroy.`

The fix is a `moved` block per copy. It tells Terraform that an object changed address and nothing else:

`moved { from = local_file.greeting[0]  to = local_file.greeting["alpha"] }`

Add one for `[1]` to `"bravo"` and one for `[2]` to `"charlie"`. The plan now shows `local_file.greeting[0] has moved to local_file.greeting["alpha"]`, three times, and `Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.` Apply, and the state uses the new addresses. Day 27 covers `moved` properly. You will use it for renames and for moving code into modules.

Two details make this safe:
- You must write one block per copy. A `moved` block cannot loop, because Terraform has to know every move before it plans.
- The old index and the new key must point at the same real object. Check the plan: each line should say "has moved to", and nothing should say "must be replaced".

The "known at plan time" rule from the count section also explains a common error. Imagine you want one container per network, and the network IDs only exist after apply. If you write `for_each = toset(docker_network.all[*].id)`, plan fails, because Terraform cannot know the keys yet. Build keys from values in your own code instead, such as the network names in a variable, and look up the IDs inside the block. Keys from your own code are known at plan time. IDs are not.

Finally, `for_each` also works on whole modules. `module "site" { for_each = var.sites ... }` makes one copy of a module per key, with addresses like `module.site["blue"]`. Day 28 builds a module and calls it more than once.

lessons.title: State: Terraform's memory
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain what Terraform's state holds, inspect it safely, rename and adopt resources with moved and import blocks, handle drift, and say where state should live in a team.

guess.q: You delete `terraform.tfstate` by mistake, while the containers it described keep running. What does the next `terraform apply` try to do?
options: Nothing: it finds them through Docker
Create everything again, as if new
Rebuild the state file from Docker
Destroy the running containers first
guess.why: Terraform only knows what it owns through the state. Without it every resource looks new, so apply tries to create them all; with Docker that fails on taken names, and in a cloud you can end up with duplicates.

terms.plain: Terraform's record of the objects a folder manages: each address, its real ID and its attributes.
The name Terraform uses for one resource, such as docker_container.web or module.dev.docker_network.app.
The first step of every plan: Terraform asks the provider about each object in state and updates its memory.
A difference between the real world and Terraform's state, usually from a change made by hand.
A block that tells Terraform an object only changed address, so it is kept instead of rebuilt.
A block that adopts an object that already exists into Terraform's state, through a normal plan and apply.
The place Terraform stores state, such as a local file, an S3 bucket or HCP Terraform.
A guard that lets only one Terraform run change a state at a time.

sections.h: Three pictures of the world
sections.body:
Terraform never looks at your cloud console or at `docker ps`. Every plan compares three pictures:
- Your code: the `.tf` files, which describe the desired state.
- The state: Terraform's memory of what it created, in `terraform.tfstate`.
- The real world: what the provider reports when Terraform asks the API.

Plan starts with a refresh. Terraform asks the provider about every object in the state and updates its memory. Then it compares that memory with your code and lists the differences. Apply makes the changes and writes the new memory.

The state's main job is a mapping from addresses to real objects: `docker_container.web` is the container with ID `d8eb279c...`. Why not just ask Docker which containers exist? Because Docker cannot tell which ones this folder owns. A container called `state-web` might be yours, a teammate's, or one from another Terraform folder. State is the list of what this folder owns, with the ID of each.

Once you see the three pictures, the rest of this lesson falls into place, because each tool fixes one link between them:
- `moved` changes an address in the state when you rename code.
- `import` adds a real object that the state does not know yet.
- Refresh-only mode copies reality into the state after someone changed things by hand.

sections.h: What is inside terraform.tfstate
sections.body:
State is a JSON file. Open it with `jq` and you find a few top-level keys:
- `version` is the file format, 4 today.
- `terraform_version` is the Terraform version that last wrote it.
- `serial` counts how many times this state has been written.
- `lineage` is an ID given when the state was first created, so two unrelated states never get mixed up.
- `resources` holds every resource, with its type, name, provider and every attribute the provider reported.

Every attribute means every attribute, secrets included. In a test, a variable marked `sensitive` went into a resource as `REDIS_PASSWORD=s3cret-123`. Plan and apply printed `(sensitive value)`, and `terraform output` printed `<sensitive>`. The state file held `"REDIS_PASSWORD=s3cret-123"` in plain text. Anyone who can read your state can read your secrets.

So never edit state by hand, never commit it, and treat it like a password file. Read it through commands instead:
- `terraform state list` prints every address.
- `terraform state show ADDRESS` prints one resource's attributes.
- `terraform show` prints everything in a readable form.

sections.h: Changing state on purpose: mv and rm
sections.body:
Two commands change state directly:
- `terraform state mv OLD NEW` gives an object a new address, right away.
- `terraform state rm ADDRESS` makes Terraform forget an object.

The name `rm` misleads people, so be clear on it: `state rm` deletes nothing real. The container keeps running, and in a cloud the server keeps running and keeps costing money. Terraform just stops tracking it. The next plan then wants to create it again, because the code still asks for it. With Docker that apply fails with `Conflict. The container name "/state-legacy" is already in use`.

Both commands act at once, with no plan and no review. That made them risky in teams, so Terraform added blocks that do the same jobs from inside your code:
- `moved` replaces `state mv`.
- `import` replaces the older `terraform import` command.
- `removed` replaces `state rm`.

A block shows up in a pull request, its effect shows up in the plan, and nothing happens until apply. Prefer the blocks, and keep the commands for emergencies.

sections.h: Renaming safely with moved blocks
sections.body:
Rename a resource label from `web` to `site`, and to Terraform you deleted one resource and wrote a new one. The plan says `docker_container.web will be destroyed (because docker_container.web is not in configuration)` and `docker_container.site will be created`. The real container would be rebuilt to change a name only you can see.

A `moved` block fixes that:

`moved { from = docker_container.web  to = docker_container.site }`

Now the plan says `docker_container.web has moved to docker_container.site` and `Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.` Apply, and the state uses the new address.

You use the same block for bigger refactors, such as moving a resource into a module on Day 28. Terraform also follows chains of moves, so a later move from `site` to somewhere else still works for a teammate who is two versions behind.

When can you delete a `moved` block? The docs call removing one a breaking change for shared modules, because anyone still on the old address would get a destroy and a create. In your own root folder it is safe once every copy of the state has been applied with the block. Keeping it costs nothing.

To stop managing something without destroying it, use a `removed` block with `lifecycle { destroy = false }`. The plan then says the object `will no longer be managed by Terraform, but will not be destroyed`.

sections.h: Adopting what already exists with import blocks
sections.body:
Sometimes the real object comes first: a bucket made in the console last year, or a container someone started by hand. An `import` block adopts it, and it takes two arguments:
- `to` is the address it should get, such as `docker_container.legacy`.
- `id` is the provider's ID for it. For a Docker container that is the full ID from `docker inspect -f '{{.Id}}' NAME`. A name does not work: the plan fails with `Cannot import non-existent remote object`.

You also write the matching `resource` block yourself. Then you plan, and here is the part that bites people. Import does not make your code match reality. If your block differs from the real object, the plan imports it and then replaces it, with `# Warning: this will destroy the imported resource`.

That warning is common with Docker, because the provider cannot read every setting back from a running container. In the worked example, three differences forced a replacement: `env`, the image written as an ID instead of a name, and `ports`. You adjust the code until the plan imports and destroys nothing. Either copy what Docker reports, or tell Terraform to ignore what it cannot read with `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [env, ports] }`.

`terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` can write a first draft of the resource block. Treat it as a draft: it lists every attribute, including defaults you do not need. Once the import is applied, the `import` block has nothing left to do, so delete it.

sections.h: Drift, and what refresh-only really does
sections.body:
Drift is any difference between the real world and Terraform's state, usually from a change made by hand. Every plan begins with a refresh, so a normal plan notices drift and proposes to undo it. In the middle of an incident that can be a surprise.

Refresh-only mode separates the two jobs:
- `terraform plan -refresh-only` shows only the changes made outside Terraform, under `Note: Objects have changed outside of Terraform`. It proposes no actions.
- `terraform apply -refresh-only` writes those changes into the state. It changes no real object.

The second one is widely misunderstood: it does not make the manual change permanent. In a test, `docker update --restart=always` changed a container by hand. After `apply -refresh-only` the state said `always`, but the code still said `no`. The very next normal plan proposed `~ restart = "always" -> "no"`. The code wins in the end.

So after drift, decide which side is right:
- The code is right: run a normal apply, and Terraform undoes the manual change.
- Reality is right: change the code to match, then apply.

Use `apply -refresh-only` when you only need the state to stop being stale, for example after someone deleted an object that the code will recreate anyway.

sections.h: Where state lives in a team
sections.body:
By default, state is a local file. That breaks as soon as a second person or a pipeline runs Terraform. Two copies drift apart, nobody has the full truth, and nothing stops two applies at once.

A **backend** decides where state is stored. A remote backend keeps one copy that everyone uses, and most of them also lock it, so only one run at a time can change the state. Start an apply in one terminal and a plan in another, and the second stops with `Error: Error acquiring the state lock`, naming the operation that holds it.

These are the common choices:
- S3 on AWS, with `use_lockfile = true`. While a run holds the lock, Terraform keeps a small `.tflock` file next to the state. Older guides lock with a DynamoDB table, which is now deprecated. The docs also strongly recommend bucket versioning, so you can roll back a bad write. Day 29 sets this up.
- HCP Terraform, HashiCorp's hosted service. Its docs say the Free plan is limited to 500 managed resources.
- Similar backends for Google Cloud Storage, Azure Storage, PostgreSQL and more.

Terraform also has better ways to keep secrets out of state. Since Terraform 1.10 a variable can be `ephemeral`: usable during a run, but never written to plan or state files. Since 1.11, some resources accept write-only arguments, such as a database password, for the same reason. OpenTofu can encrypt the whole state file. The Go deeper section shows all three.

lessons.analogy: State is like the ticket book in a theatre cloakroom. When you hand in a coat, the attendant writes your ticket number next to a hook. Without the book there is a room full of coats and no way to know which ones are yours, and a new attendant would hang a second copy of everything. The comparison has a limit: the book only notes the hook, while Terraform's state copies every detail of each object, secrets included.

task.title: State surgery on infra/local: rename, drift, import, retire
steps: Bring `infra/local` up to date with the Day 26 files, build the image if needed (`docker build -t hello-devops:1.0.0 .` in the repo root), and apply. `curl localhost:8080` a few times.
Explore the state: run `terraform state list`, `terraform state show docker_container.redis` and `jq .serial terraform.tfstate`.

Rename `docker_container.web` to `docker_container.app`, and fix the reference in `outputs.tf`. Plan once without a `moved` block and read the destroy. Then add the block from the Files section and plan until it says "has moved to". Apply.
Cause drift: `docker rm -f hello-redis`. Check that `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' localhost:8080/readyz` prints 503.
Run `terraform plan -refresh-only`, then a normal `terraform apply`. Is `/readyz` back to 200? What happened to the `visits` count, and why?

A teammate starts a Redis by hand: `docker run -d --name hello-redis-tmp redis:8-alpine`. Create `imported.tf` with an import block (the ID from `docker inspect`) and a `docker_container.redis_tmp` resource.
Plan. If it says "must be replaced", change your resource block until the plan says "will be updated in-place" or "will be imported" with 0 to destroy. Then apply.
Retire it the Terraform way: delete `imported.tf`, plan (expect 1 to destroy) and apply. Check that `docker ps` no longer lists hello-redis-tmp.
Finish with `terraform plan`. Commit `main.tf` and `outputs.tf`.
hints: Docker reports the image by the name you typed in `docker run`, so `image = docker_image.redis.name` matches and `image_id` does not.
The Docker provider cannot read `env` back from a running container. `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [env] }` stops that one difference from forcing a replacement.
Terraform recreated the Redis container, not the data inside it. The lab's Redis has no volume.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate wants to commit `terraform.tfstate` so everyone can share it. In 3 to 4 sentences, explain what state contains, why it matters, and where it should live instead.
explain_back.answer: The state file is Terraform's record of what this folder manages: it links each address in our code to a real object ID and stores every attribute. Plan depends on it to decide what to create, change or destroy, so a lost or stale copy causes real damage. It can hold secrets in plain text, even values marked sensitive, which rules out git, and git cannot lock it either. It belongs in a remote backend such as a versioned S3 bucket with `use_lockfile = true`, so there is one copy and only one run changes it at a time.

recap: Plan compares three pictures: your code, the state and the real world, refreshed from the provider.
State maps addresses to real IDs and holds every attribute, secrets included, in plain text.
`moved` renames without rebuilding, `import` adopts, and `removed` forgets; all of them show up in the plan.
Read every import plan: "must be replaced" means your code does not match the real object yet.
`apply -refresh-only` updates state only; the next normal apply still enforces the code.
Teams keep state in a locked remote backend, such as S3 with `use_lockfile = true`, and never in git.

check.q: You mark a variable `db_password` as `sensitive = true` and pass it to a resource. Where can someone still read the real value?
options: Nowhere: Terraform encrypts it
Only in the plan output
Only inside the provider
In the state file, in plain text
check.why: `sensitive` only hides the value in Terraform's output; the state still stores it as plain text.

check.q: Someone runs `docker update --restart=always` on a container that your code declares with `restart = "no"`. You run `terraform apply -refresh-only`, then `terraform plan`. What does the plan show?
options: No changes, because the state now matches
An update that sets restart back to no
A replacement of the whole container
An error saying the state is stale
check.why: Refresh-only copied the drift into state, but the code still says `no`, so the next normal plan changes it back.

check.q: You run `terraform state rm docker_container.redis` and then `terraform apply`. The container is still running. What happens?
options: Apply tries to create it and fails on the name
Terraform finds the container and adopts it
Terraform deletes the running container
Nothing, because the code did not change
check.why: `state rm` only made Terraform forget; the code still asks for the container, so apply tries to create it and Docker refuses the duplicate name.

interview.q: How do you manage Terraform state in a team?
interview.a: I keep it in a remote backend, such as a versioned and encrypted S3 bucket with `use_lockfile = true`, or HCP Terraform. Locking means only one run changes a state at a time. I limit who can read and write it, because it holds secrets, and usually only the pipeline may write. I split large setups into several states, one per environment or component, so a mistake has a smaller blast radius. Changes to addresses go through `moved`, `import` and `removed` blocks in pull requests, not hand edits.

interview.q: What is drift, and how do you handle it?
interview.a: Drift is a difference between the real infrastructure and Terraform's state, usually from a manual change or another tool. A normal plan shows it and proposes to undo it, and `plan -refresh-only` shows only the outside changes. Then I decide which side is right. Either I apply to restore the code, or I change the code to match reality. `apply -refresh-only` only updates the state, so the code still wins on the next apply. A scheduled refresh-only plan in CI catches drift early.

interview.q: How do you bring existing infrastructure under Terraform?
interview.a: I write an `import` block with the target address and the provider's ID, plus a resource block that describes the object. `plan -generate-config-out` can draft that block. Then I plan and iterate until the plan says the object will be imported with nothing destroyed, because a mismatch shows up as "must be replaced". After apply I delete the import block. For many resources, newer Terraform versions can also discover them in bulk with `terraform query`.

deeper.body:
State holds every attribute, so it holds every secret that passes through a resource. Terraform gives you several tools, and they do different jobs.

1. `sensitive = true` on a variable or output hides the value in plan, apply and output, and that is all. The value is still in the state in plain text. It is still worth using, because it keeps secrets out of CI logs.
2. `ephemeral = true` on a variable (Terraform 1.10 and later) makes the value exist only during the run. It is never written to plan or state files, and Terraform enforces that. In a test, an ephemeral variable passed into an ordinary argument failed the plan with `Ephemeral values are not valid for "input", because it is not a write-only attribute and must be persisted to state.`
3. Write-only arguments (Terraform 1.11 and later) are arguments a provider sends to the API but never stores. The docs' example gives an AWS database its password through `password_wo`, generated by an `ephemeral "random_password"` block. Terraform never stores the value, so it cannot tell when it changed. You bump a number in a second argument, `password_wo_version`, to send a new password.
4. An `ephemeral` resource block, like `ephemeral "random_password"`, produces a value that only lives during the run, so the secret never touches state.

Not every provider supports write-only arguments yet, so check the provider's docs for each secret you handle.

Then protect the state itself, because it will still hold IDs, addresses and whatever else a provider returns:
- Keep it in a remote backend that encrypts at rest, such as S3 with server-side encryption.
- Limit who can read it. Reading state is close to reading production.
- On OpenTofu, turn on state encryption. An `encryption` block inside `terraform` encrypts state and plan files with a key from a passphrase or a key service such as AWS KMS.

Which tool should you reach for first? Keep secrets out of `.tf` files and committed `.tfvars` files, always. Mark anything secret as `sensitive`. Where your Terraform and provider versions allow it, pass secrets as ephemeral values into write-only arguments, so they never reach the state. And whatever is left, protect by protecting the state.

lessons.title: Modules and environments
lessons.goal: By the end you can write a small module with inputs and outputs, call it more than once, choose a layout for environments, and test a module with terraform test.

guess.q: Your dev and prod environments need different credentials and access rules. Which setup does HashiCorp's documentation recommend?
options: Two CLI workspaces in one folder
One folder with a tfvars file each
A folder per environment calling shared modules
Copying the whole folder and editing it
guess.why: CLI workspaces share one backend, so the docs call them unsuitable for isolation; a separate root per environment that calls shared modules gets its own backend and permissions.

terms.plain: A folder of .tf files. Another folder can call it with a module block, like a function.
The folder where you run terraform; it calls child modules and owns the state.
A folder called from a module block, with variables as inputs and outputs as return values.
Where a module lives: a local path, a registry address or a git URL.
A second, separate state for the same folder of code, chosen with terraform workspace.
Terraform's test runner. It runs run blocks from .tftest.hcl files and checks assert conditions.
A fake provider in tests that invents computed values, so tests create nothing real.

sections.h: Every folder is a module
sections.body:
You have written modules since Day 25 without the word. A **module** is a folder of `.tf` files. The folder where you run `terraform` is the root module. When it calls another folder with a `module` block, that folder becomes a child module. Shortened, a call looks like this: `module "dev" { source = "../modules/hello-stack"  name = "hello"  host_port = 8080 }`.

Think of a child module as a Kotlin function:
- Its variables are the parameters. Those without a default are required.
- Its outputs are the return values, read as `module.dev.url`.
- Its resources are the side effects. Call it twice and you get two sets of real objects.

The comparison breaks in one place. A function call is gone when it returns, but a module call lives on in the state. Its resources get addresses with a module prefix, such as `module.dev.docker_container.app`, and they stay until you remove the call.

After you add or change a `module` block, run `terraform init` again. It records where each module lives, and it downloads remote modules into `.terraform/modules`. Local folders are used in place. You can see what init found in `.terraform/modules/modules.json`, which lists each call and its folder. If you forget init, plan stops with `Error: Module not installed` and tells you to run it.

refs.title: Complete Terraform course: modules and multiple environments (DevOps Directive)

sections.h: Designing a module's inputs and outputs
sections.body:
A module's variables are its API, so design them like one:
- Ask only for what really changes between calls. hello-stack takes a name prefix, a port, the app image and version, an optional greeting and the Redis image ID.
- Give a default only where one value suits almost everyone, like `greeting = ""`.
- Validate inside the module. `host_port` rejects ports below 1024 there, so every caller gets the check for free.
- Return what callers need, such as the URL and the container names, and nothing more.

A child module names its providers in `required_providers`, but it has no `provider` block. The root configures each provider once, and every module call uses it. Write the module's constraint loosely, like `>= 4.6, < 5.0`, and let the root pin the exact version.

Names need care when one module is called twice. Docker refuses two containers with the same name, and clouds refuse two buckets with the same name. The hello-stack module builds every name from `var.name`, so the dev stack gets `hello-web` and the test stack gets `hello-test-web`.

The usual layout is four files, `main.tf`, `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf` and `versions.tf`, plus a README when other teams use the module. HashiCorp's style guide keeps local modules in a `modules` folder. The lab puts it in `infra/modules/hello-stack`, next to the `local` and `aws` roots, so any root can call it.

sections.h: Where modules come from, and pinning them
sections.body:
The `source` argument says where a module lives:
- A local path that starts with `./` or `../`. Terraform uses the folder in place, and a change shows up on the next plan.
- The public registry, such as `terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws`, with a separate `version` argument like `version = "~> 6.7"`.
- A git repository, such as `git::https://example.com/acme/tf-modules.git//vpc?ref=v1.2.0`, where `?ref=` pins a tag or a commit.

Registry modules save real work. The [terraform-aws-modules VPC module](https://github.com/terraform-aws-modules/terraform-aws-vpc) builds a whole network with subnets and gateways from a handful of arguments. Remember that a module runs with your permissions and creates real, billed resources. Read one before you use it, the way you would read a library before adding it to `build.gradle.kts`.

Pin every remote module. HashiCorp's style guide says to pin modules to a specific major and minor version, because an unpinned module can change your infrastructure on the next `init`. To move to a newer version, change the constraint, run `terraform init -upgrade`, and read the plan before you apply.

sections.h: Small modules, composed in a thin root
sections.body:
How big should a module be? Draw the line around something one team owns and changes as a unit, like "one hello-devops stack" or "one service's database". Avoid both extremes:
- A module that wraps a single resource adds a layer to read and saves nothing.
- One giant module for the whole company puts everything at risk on every change, and its plans take minutes.

Composition means wiring small modules together in the root, instead of nesting them deeply. Data flows through arguments and outputs. In the lab, the root owns the Redis image and passes its ID into both stacks. The module does not create the image itself, because two stacks would then manage the same image twice.

A good root module ends up short. It configures providers, calls modules, and connects outputs to inputs. HashiCorp's docs describe each environment the same way: a backend block plus a small number of module blocks, with arguments for the few things that differ. Free advice from many teams: if your root folder grows past a few hundred lines, look for a module hiding in it.

sections.h: Environments: workspaces, folders or tfvars files
sections.body:
Dev, test and prod need the same shape with small differences. Teams handle that in three ways:
1. One folder, several workspaces. `terraform workspace new qa` gives the same code a second, empty state, and `terraform.workspace` holds the current name.
2. One folder, one `.tfvars` file per environment, used as `terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars`. Each environment still needs its own state, so you also switch backend settings per environment, which is easy to get wrong.
3. One folder per environment, like `envs/dev` and `envs/prod`. Each is a short root that calls shared modules and has its own backend and state.

HashiCorp's own docs lean towards the third. They say CLI workspaces share one backend, so they are not a suitable isolation mechanism when environments need separate credentials and access controls. Prod should not share a bucket, or a set of permissions, with someone's experiment.

So most teams use a folder per long-lived environment, with differences kept in a few module arguments. Workspaces are still handy for short-lived copies, such as one stack per feature branch. They need care, though: the worked example shows a fresh workspace planning to create containers whose names and ports are already taken. If you use workspaces, build names from `terraform.workspace`, such as `name = "site-${terraform.workspace}"`, and look up ports in a map keyed by workspace. With the S3 backend, each extra workspace's state is stored under `env:/<workspace>/` in the same bucket, next to the default one.

sections.h: Testing modules with terraform test
sections.body:
A module is code, so it deserves tests. `terraform test` runs files that end in `.tftest.hcl`, usually from a `tests` folder inside the module. A test file holds one or more `run` blocks:
- `command = plan` checks the plan only, like a unit test. Nothing is created.
- `command = apply` is the default. It creates real resources, checks them, and destroys them when the file finishes, like an integration test.
- An `assert` block holds a `condition` and an `error_message`.
- A `variables` block sets inputs for the whole file or for one run.
- `expect_failures` says a run must fail, such as `expect_failures = [var.host_port]` to prove that port 80 is rejected.

A `mock_provider "docker" {}` block swaps the real provider for a fake one that invents values for computed attributes. Then even `command = apply` creates nothing, and the tests need no Docker and no cloud account. That makes them cheap enough to run on every pull request, which Day 29 does.

The lab's test file has five runs: three check names and settings, one checks the `url` output, and one proves that port 80 is rejected. When a run fails, the output shows the actual and the expected value side by side, so you see the problem without guessing. Run the tests after every change to the module, the way you run unit tests after changing a class.

sections.h: Before every push: fmt, validate and tflint
sections.body:
Three cheap checks catch most problems before a plan:
- `terraform fmt -recursive` rewrites every file in the standard style. In CI you run `terraform fmt -check -recursive`, which fails instead of rewriting.
- `terraform validate` checks syntax, types and references, with no credentials and without touching anything.
- tflint is a separate linter with more rules. Its built-in rules catch things like unused variables and providers with no version constraint. Plugins add provider rules, such as the AWS plugin spotting an instance type that does not exist, which `validate` cannot know.

Install tflint with `brew install --cask terraform-linters/tap/tflint`, as its README says. Run `tflint --init` once to download the plugins named in `.tflint.hcl`, then run `tflint` in a folder, or `tflint --recursive` from the top.

Run all three before you push. Day 29 puts them into the pipeline, in front of a security scanner and the AWS plan.

task.title: Turn infra/local into a module used twice
steps: Create `infra/modules/hello-stack/` with a `versions.tf` that only lists the docker provider. Add a `variables.tf` for the name prefix, host port (with validation), app image, app version, greeting and Redis image ID.

explain_back.prompt: In 3 to 4 sentences, explain to a teammate how one module can create both a dev and a test stack without them colliding. Mention inputs, outputs and resource addresses.
explain_back.answer: The module is one folder of code with variables as its inputs and outputs as its return values. The root calls it twice, as `module.dev` and `module.test`, with different inputs such as the name prefix and the port. Every name inside is built from the name input, so Docker gets `hello-web` and `hello-test-web`, and each call's resources get their own addresses in the state. Changing the module's code changes both stacks on the next apply, which is the point.

Variables are a module's API, outputs its return values, and resources get addresses like `module.dev.docker_container.app`.

Keep modules focused and roots thin: providers, module calls and wiring.
Prefer a folder per long-lived environment over CLI workspaces when credentials differ.

interview.q: What is a Terraform module, and when do you write one?
interview.a: A module is a folder of Terraform code with input variables and outputs, called from another configuration with a `module` block. I write one when the same shape of infrastructure appears more than once, such as a service stack per environment, or when a team wants a reviewed, versioned building block. I keep modules focused on one unit of ownership, not one resource. I pin remote modules to a version and test shared ones with `terraform test`.

interview.q: How do you manage dev, staging and prod with Terraform?
interview.a: I put the shared shape into modules and give each long-lived environment its own small root folder with its own backend, state and credentials. The differences live in a few module arguments or a small tfvars file per folder. HashiCorp's docs say CLI workspaces share a backend and are not a suitable isolation mechanism for environments with different access controls. Changes roll through dev first, then prod, often by bumping a module version.

interview.q: How do you test Terraform code?
interview.a: First the cheap checks: `terraform fmt -check`, `terraform validate` and tflint, plus a security scanner such as trivy. Then `terraform test` with `.tftest.hcl` files: plan-mode runs for logic and naming, `expect_failures` for validation rules, and mock providers so the tests need no cloud account. For important modules I add an apply-mode test against a real sandbox account, which creates and destroys real resources. And every pull request still gets a human reading the real plan.

deeper.body:
Once other teams use your module, it becomes a product with users, and changes need the care you give a library.

Version it with git tags and semantic versioning. A new optional input is a minor version, like v1.3.0. A renamed input, a removed output, or anything that replaces resources is a major version, like v2.0.0. Callers pin with `?ref=v1.3.0` in a git source, or with `version = "~> 1.3"` for a registry module. HashiCorp's style guide names registry module repos `terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME>`, such as `terraform-aws-vpc`.

Refactors inside a module need `moved` blocks too, and they belong in the module itself. Say version 2 renames `docker_container.app` to `docker_container.web`. A `moved` block inside the module turns that into a move for every caller, on their next apply. The refactoring docs strongly recommend keeping old `moved` blocks in shared modules, because removing one breaks anyone still upgrading from an older version.

Test where your users will feel it:
- Plan-mode tests with a mock provider for naming, validation and wiring. They are fast and need no credentials.
- An apply-mode test against a sandbox account for anything subtle, such as IAM policies. It costs a little time and money, so many teams run it nightly instead of on every push.
- An `examples` folder with a small root that calls the module. It doubles as documentation and as an extra check that the module really works from the outside.

Two bigger tools exist once a company has many environments. HCP Terraform has Stacks, which describe repeated deployments of the same components with `component` and `deployment` blocks, each deployment with its own state. Some teams use a wrapper tool to generate many small roots from one template. Neither is needed for this course. Folders, modules and pinned versions carry you a long way, and they work the same in Terraform and OpenTofu.

lessons.title: Terraform on a real cloud, and in CI
lessons.goal: By the end you can set up a safe AWS account, create a private S3 bucket with Terraform, keep state in it, and run checks, plan and apply from GitHub Actions without stored keys.

Nothing: free usage goes on for another year
The account closes unless you upgrade to a paid plan

guess.why: The Free plan does not charge you. When the credits or the six months run out, the account closes, and you have 90 days to upgrade if you want to keep it.

terms.plain: AWS's service for users, roles and permissions, which decides who can do what.
A set of AWS permissions that a person or a program can borrow for a short time.
A standard that lets one system, such as GitHub, prove who it is to another with a short-lived signed token.
The part of an IAM role that says who may use the role, for example one GitHub repo.

sections.h: Before any cloud: make the account safe
sections.body:
Everything on AWS today is optional. The rest of the course runs on your laptop, and the worked example below needs no account. Day 10 explained cloud costs and free plans. This is the checklist to finish before your first apply, in order:
1. Sign up and choose the Free plan. Accounts created since July 15, 2025 pick a plan. The Free plan gives up to $200 in credits for six months and cannot charge your card. When the credits or the six months run out, the account closes, and you have 90 days to upgrade if you want it back.
2. Protect the root user, the email login you signed up with. It can do anything, even close the account. Turn on MFA for it and never use it for daily work.
3. In Billing and Cost Management, open Budgets and create a zero spend budget from a template. It emails you once your spending goes above the free usage.
4. Make an everyday login that is not root (next section).

Older accounts stay on the previous free tier and can be billed, so the budget matters even more there. Also, do not create an AWS Organization on a learning account: AWS lists joining Organizations among the actions that move a Free plan account to the Paid plan.

A budget alert only sends email. It stops nothing, and its numbers can lag by hours. Destroying what you create is what protects you, and it is the last step today. IAM roles and the OIDC provider cost nothing. S3 charges per gigabyte stored each month plus a little per request, and a state file is a few kilobytes, so today's bucket costs close to nothing. Check the S3 pricing page for your Region anyway.

sections.h: A login for your laptop that is not root
sections.body:
Terraform's AWS provider finds credentials the same way as the AWS CLI. Its docs list the order. Arguments in the provider block come first, then environment variables such as `AWS_PROFILE`, then the shared files in `~/.aws`. Last come the credentials of a container or a machine running in AWS. Install the CLI with `brew install awscli`, and check the current AWS docs if anything differs.

You have two common ways to get a login that is not root:
- IAM Identity Center, AWS's single sign-on. You sign in through the browser and get short-lived credentials. Run `aws configure sso` once, then `aws sso login` each day.
- An IAM user with MFA and an access key, saved with `aws configure`. It is simpler, but the key is a long-lived password on your disk. Delete it when you finish.

Identity Center is the better habit, with one catch. It is built on AWS Organizations, which would move a Free plan account to the Paid plan. To stay on the Free plan, use the IAM user today and delete its key tonight.

Then run `aws sts get-caller-identity`. It should print your 12-digit account ID and a user or role that is not root. If that works, Terraform will work too, because it reads the same credentials. Never put an access key into a `.tf` file or a `.tfvars` file.

sections.h: A private, versioned bucket, then state inside it
sections.body:
The lab's `infra/aws` folder creates one S3 bucket. A bucket name must be unique across every AWS account in the world, so the code adds your 12-digit account ID to it. It reads that ID with the data source `aws_caller_identity`. A data source reads something that exists without managing it.

In the AWS provider, a bucket's settings are separate resources that sit next to `aws_s3_bucket`:
- `aws_s3_bucket_versioning` keeps every old version of every file, so you can undo a bad write.
- `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` stops anything in the bucket from becoming public.
- `aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration` encrypts files with keys that S3 manages.

New buckets already block public access and encrypt files by default. Write it down anyway, so reviewers and scanners can see it. The provider's `default_tags` block adds tags such as `Project` and `ManagedBy` to every resource, so you can always tell what something is for.

This bucket also stores its own state, which sounds impossible at first: Terraform needs the bucket to store state, but the bucket does not exist until Terraform creates it. You solve it in two steps:
1. Apply with local state. This creates the bucket.
2. Uncomment the `backend "s3"` block, put in the bucket name, and run `terraform init -migrate-state`. Terraform copies the state into S3 and uses it from then on.

The block sets `use_lockfile = true`, which you met on Day 27. Each run writes a small `.tflock` file next to the state, and a second run that finds it stops with a lock error.

sections.h: GitHub Actions logs in to AWS with OIDC
sections.body:
On Day 21 you met OIDC: a workflow gets a short-lived token from GitHub instead of storing cloud keys. The lab's `github-oidc.tf` builds the AWS side:
1. An OIDC identity provider for `token.actions.githubusercontent.com` with the audience `sts.amazonaws.com`.
2. An IAM role whose **trust policy** checks the token's `sub` (subject) claim. It names your repo and the context, such as `pull_request` or `environment:production`.
3. A permissions policy that says what the role may do.

The `sub` has to match exactly, character for character. Repos created after July 15, 2026 put numeric IDs in it, like `repo:you@123456/hello-devops@456789:pull_request`. Older repos use `repo:you/hello-devops:pull_request`. The lab trusts both forms, for your repo only. When the login fails with "Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", check the `sub` first.

Keep the role small. The lab's role may manage only buckets whose names start with `hello-devops-`, and read its own IAM setup so that plan works. It cannot change IAM, so a pull request cannot give the pipeline more power. You apply IAM changes from your laptop.
