sections.h: The pipeline: checks, plan on pull requests, apply on main
sections.body:
The lab's `.github/workflows/terraform.yml` runs when anything under `infra/` changes. It has three jobs:
1. `checks` runs on every pull request and push, with no cloud login. It runs `terraform fmt -check`, tflint, a trivy scan, `terraform validate` for `infra/local` and `infra/aws`, and the hello-stack module's tests with the mock provider from Day 28.
2. `plan` runs on pull requests once the checks pass. It logs in to AWS with OIDC, runs `terraform plan -out=tfplan`, and puts the plan on the run's summary page for reviewers.
3. `apply` runs after a merge to main. It waits in the `production` environment until a required reviewer approves, then plans and applies.

The cheap checks run first, so a formatting slip fails before anything logs in to AWS. The AWS jobs also have `vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN != ''` in their `if`. Until you save the role ARN as a repository variable, they are skipped, so a repo without an AWS account still gets green checks.

A few more settings are worth spotting:
- `concurrency` with `cancel-in-progress: false` on the AWS jobs, so a second run waits and never stops an apply halfway.
- `TF_VAR_` environment variables filled from the `github` context, so CI passes your owner, repo and their IDs without any secrets.
- `id-token: write` only on the two jobs that log in to AWS. The checks job can only read the repo.
- Third-party actions pinned to full commit SHAs, as on Day 21.

refs.title: OpenID Connect in GitHub Actions (GitHub docs)
Complete Terraform course: AWS and GitHub Actions (DevOps Directive)

sections.h: Linters and scanners, and trusting the scanner
sections.body:
Plan tells you what will change. It does not tell you whether the change is wise. Three free tools help:
- tflint, from Day 28, finds mistakes that `validate` misses. The lab's `infra/aws/.tflint.hcl` turns on its AWS plugin, which knows real AWS values.
- `trivy config` looks for security problems, such as public buckets, missing encryption, or IAM policies that allow too much. It took over from tfsec, whose README asks users to move to Trivy.
- checkov does a similar job with over 1000 built-in policies, and it can scan GitHub Actions workflows too.

Scanners are strict on purpose, and you decide what to fix. To accept a finding, put a comment such as `# trivy:ignore:AWS-0132` above the resource, followed by your reason. A reviewer can then read the decision and question it.

A scanner is also software that runs with access to your code, and sometimes to your secrets. In March 2026 attackers moved most version tags of `aquasecurity/trivy-action` to malicious code, tracked as CVE-2026-33634. Any workflow that used the action through one of those tags ran the attacker's code. The lab's Terraform workflow runs the trivy image pinned to a digest, and its release workflow pins trivy-action to a full commit SHA. Day 52 tells the whole story.

code.src:
name: terraform

on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["infra/**", ".github/workflows/terraform.yml"]
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["infra/**", ".github/workflows/terraform.yml"]

# Default for every job: the GITHUB_TOKEN can only read the repository.
permissions:
  contents: read

env:
  AWS_REGION: us-east-1 # same Region as infra/aws/variables.tf and the backend block
  TF_IN_AUTOMATION: "true"
  # Values for infra/aws/variables.tf, taken from the github context.
  TF_VAR_github_owner: ${{ github.repository_owner }}
  TF_VAR_github_owner_id: ${{ github.repository_owner_id }}
  TF_VAR_github_repo: ${{ github.event.repository.name }}
  TF_VAR_github_repo_id: ${{ github.repository_id }}

jobs:
  # Checks that need no cloud account. They run on every pull request and push.
  checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: infra
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      # Third-party actions are pinned to a full commit SHA (Day 21).
      # The comment shows the version. Dependabot keeps both up to date.
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@dfe3c3f87815947d99a8997f908cb6525fc44e9e # v4.0.1
        with:
          terraform_version: "1.17.1"
          terraform_wrapper: false

      - name: Formatting
        run: terraform fmt -check -recursive

      - uses: terraform-linters/setup-tflint@6ffdbaa3be476b3431f7275c26966ef32ff60337 # v6.3.2
        with:
          tflint_version: v0.65.0
      - name: Lint (tflint, in every folder under infra)
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }} # avoids rate limits when tflint downloads plugins
        run: |
          tflint --recursive --init
          tflint --recursive --format compact

      # The trivy image is pinned to a digest, not a tag. In March 2026 attackers
      # moved most tags of aquasecurity/trivy-action to malicious code (Day 52).
      - name: Scan for risky settings (trivy)
        run: >-
          docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/src:ro"
          aquasec/trivy:0.76.0@sha256:2416d1f74045b57274df1a340eee6b510cacd73c66a6ccb8da092b117eb7d222
          config --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL /src

      - name: Validate the local stack and the aws folder
        run: |
          terraform -chdir=local init -backend=false -input=false
          terraform -chdir=local validate
          terraform -chdir=aws init -backend=false -input=false
          terraform -chdir=aws validate

      - name: Test the hello-stack module (a mock Docker, nothing is created)
        run: |
          terraform -chdir=modules/hello-stack init -input=false
          terraform -chdir=modules/hello-stack test

  # Plan the AWS folder on pull requests. Skipped until you set the
  # repository variable AWS_ROLE_ARN (Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions).
  plan:
    needs: checks
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request' && vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN != ''
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write # lets this job ask GitHub for an OIDC token
    # One AWS run at a time. Never cancel a run halfway through.
    concurrency:
      group: terraform-aws
      cancel-in-progress: false
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: infra/aws
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@dfe3c3f87815947d99a8997f908cb6525fc44e9e # v4.0.1
        with:
          terraform_version: "1.17.1"
          terraform_wrapper: false
      # Log in to AWS with OIDC: short-lived credentials, no stored keys.
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@e1253824e5c10ff9df46874f81ed3ec929e19cfd # v6.3.0
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN }}
          aws-region: ${{ env.AWS_REGION }}
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - run: terraform plan -input=false -no-color -out=tfplan
      - name: Show the plan on the run's summary page
        run: |
          {
            echo '```'
            terraform show -no-color tfplan
            echo '```'
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

  # Apply on main after the merge, behind the production environment.
  apply:
    needs: checks
    if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN != ''
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    environment: production # waits here until a required reviewer approves
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write
    concurrency:
      group: terraform-aws
      cancel-in-progress: false
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: infra/aws
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@dfe3c3f87815947d99a8997f908cb6525fc44e9e # v4.0.1
        with:
          terraform_version: "1.17.1"
          terraform_wrapper: false
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@e1253824e5c10ff9df46874f81ed3ec929e19cfd # v6.3.0
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN }}
          aws-region: ${{ env.AWS_REGION }}
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - run: terraform plan -input=false -no-color -out=tfplan
      - run: terraform apply -input=false -no-color tfplan

explain_back.prompt: In 3 to 4 sentences, explain how your workflow gets permission to change AWS without any stored keys. Mention the OIDC provider, the trust policy and the `sub` claim.
explain_back.answer: The job has `id-token: write`, so it can ask GitHub for a signed OIDC token. The configure-aws-credentials action sends that token to AWS and asks to use our IAM role. AWS checks the signature through the OIDC provider for token.actions.githubusercontent.com, and the role's trust policy checks the `aud` and `sub` claims. The `sub` names our repo and the context, such as a pull request or the production environment, so no other repo can use the role. If everything matches, AWS returns credentials that expire after a short time.

check.q: Your pull request's plan job passes the checks, then fails with "Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity". What is the most likely cause?
options: The bucket name is already taken
The token's `sub` does not match the trust policy
terraform fmt changed a file during the run
The budget alert blocked the request
check.why: That error means AWS refused the token for this role, which almost always means the `sub` or `aud` condition did not match.

check.q: You want CI to apply only after a person says yes. Where does that gate live in the lab?
options: In the production environment's required reviewers
In the S3 backend's lock file
In the trust policy's `aud` condition
In the workflow's concurrency group
check.why: A job with `environment: production` waits until a required reviewer of that environment approves it.

check.q: A teammate adds `Owner = "ops"` to the provider's `default_tags` in a pull request. The plan looks fine, but apply on main fails. Why?
options: Tags cannot change once a bucket exists
The saved plan expired before apply
S3 buckets do not support tags
Default tags also change the IAM role
check.why: The CI role can read IAM but not change it, so tag updates on the IAM role and OIDC provider are refused at apply time.

interview.q: How would you run Terraform safely in CI/CD?
interview.a: Run fmt, validate, a linter, module tests and a security scanner on every pull request, then a plan that reviewers can read. Apply only from the main branch, behind an approval such as a protected environment, with one run at a time. Keep state in a remote backend with locking, and log in with OIDC so there are no long-lived cloud keys. Give the CI role the smallest permissions it needs, keep powerful changes such as IAM out of the automatic path, and pin third-party actions to commit SHAs.

interview.q: Why use OIDC instead of AWS access keys stored in GitHub secrets?
interview.a: Access keys last until someone deletes them, so a key that leaks through a log or a compromised action can be used for months. With OIDC, the job gets a signed token from GitHub and swaps it for AWS credentials that expire within hours. The role's trust policy limits which repo, branch or environment may get them. There is also nothing to store or rotate.

interview.q: Why pin a GitHub Action to a commit SHA instead of a tag like v4?
interview.a: A tag is a movable pointer, so whoever controls the action's repo can point it at different code later. In March 2026 attackers did exactly that to most tags of `aquasecurity/trivy-action`, and every workflow that used those tags ran their code. A full commit SHA cannot be moved, so you run the code you reviewed. A version comment next to the SHA and Dependabot keep pinned actions readable and up to date.

deeper.body:
The lab's pipeline leaves three gaps that real teams usually close.

First, the plan you reviewed is not exactly the plan that runs. The pull request's plan is made from the branch, before the merge. The apply job makes a fresh plan from main, which may include other merged changes or new drift. Teams handle this in a few ways:
- Require pull request branches to be up to date with main before merging, so the reviewed plan is closer to what runs.
- Split the work on main into two jobs. One plans and saves the plan file as an artifact. The next one, behind the environment gate, applies exactly that file, so the approver can read it first.
- Use a tool built for this. Atlantis is open source and runs plan and apply from pull request comments. HCP Terraform and similar services do the same as a hosted product.

Second, one role for both jobs gives a pull request more power than it needs. A cleaner design has two roles. The plan role trusts only `pull_request` and gets read-only permissions, plus access to the state and lock files. The apply role trusts only `environment:production` and may change things. This matters because anyone who can push a branch could edit the workflow in a pull request to run apply.

Third, access to state is a permission in itself. Anyone who can write the state bucket can change what Terraform believes exists. Big teams keep state buckets in a separate account. They turn on versioning and `prevent_destroy`, and only a few roles may write. Each environment gets its own state file, and often its own account, so a mistake in the dev state cannot touch production.

Teams also use destroy outside labs. They run short-lived test environments and destroy them automatically each night. Because the code describes everything, one apply brings them back in the morning, and the same `terraform test` suite from Day 28 checks that the modules still build what they promise.

quiz.q: A plan line ends with `# forces replacement`. What will apply do to that resource?
options: Edit it in place
Destroy it and create a new one
Skip it until next time
Import it into the state
quiz.why: Terraform cannot change that attribute on the existing object, so it destroys the object and creates a new one.

quiz.q: Which statement about Terraform state is true?
options: It is a cache you can delete safely
Terraform encrypts it on your laptop
You should commit it so teammates share it
It can contain secrets in plain text
quiz.why: State stores every attribute, passwords and tokens included, so protect it and keep it in a proper backend.

quiz.q: Two pipeline runs try to apply against the same S3-backed state at the same moment. What stops them from corrupting it?
options: The lock file from `use_lockfile = true`
The `-refresh-only` flag
Bucket versioning on its own
The `.terraform.lock.hcl` file
quiz.why: With `use_lockfile = true`, the first run holds a lock file and the second is refused; `.terraform.lock.hcl` only pins provider versions.

quiz.q: What does `[for s in ["a", "b", "c"] : upper(s) if s != "b"]` evaluate to?
quiz.why: The `if` drops "b", `upper` changes the rest, and square brackets build a list.

quiz.q: You move three resources into `module.dev`, and the plan says 3 to add and 3 to destroy. What is missing?
options: A `terraform init -upgrade`
An import block for each resource
`moved` blocks from the old to the new addresses
A `removed` block for each resource
quiz.why: Without `moved` blocks Terraform sees old addresses vanish and new ones appear; with them the plan shows moves and 0 to destroy.

quiz.q: Which `terraform test` setup checks a module without creating any real resources?
options: `command = plan` runs, or a mock provider
`command = apply` runs with the real provider
A run block that only calls validate
A workspace named test
quiz.why: Plan-mode runs create nothing, and a mock provider makes even apply-mode runs fake.

quiz.q: In the lab, the CI role may not change IAM. So how do changes to the role itself get applied?
options: By the plan job on pull requests
By the apply job after approval
By a nightly drift job
From your laptop, with your own login
quiz.why: Keeping IAM changes out of CI means a pull request cannot give the pipeline more power.

quiz.q: You applied with `-var host_port=9000` yesterday. Today you run `terraform plan` with no flags and no tfvars file. What do you see?
options: No changes, because Terraform remembers 9000
A plan that moves the app back to the default port
An error that asks you for host_port
A plan to destroy everything
quiz.why: Terraform does not remember `-var` values, so today's plan uses the default and proposes to change the port back.

quiz.q: In `infra/local`, the app reaches Redis at the host name `hello-redis`. Which Docker feature makes that work?
options: Port mapping with `-p`
A bind mount
DNS on a user-defined network
The HEALTHCHECK instruction
quiz.why: Containers on the same user-defined network find each other by container name through Docker's built-in DNS.

quiz.q: A job uses `environment: production`, and that environment has a required reviewer. What happens when the job is triggered?
options: It runs, then asks for a review afterwards
It fails, because environments need secrets
It runs only on pull requests
It waits until a reviewer approves it
quiz.why: Required reviewers are a protection rule: the job pauses before it starts until someone approves.
